narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your LSAT score, your undergraduate GPA, and your academic performance in the third year of law school. 

Your LSAT score of 39 was the strongest influence, and it actually worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was outweighed by the other two factors. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average among students who were accepted, and this pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Similarly, finishing in the fourth decile for third-year grades (compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students) added further weight toward predicting that you would not pass the bar on the first try.

Taken together, these academic performance signals led the model to conclude that the risk of first-time failure was too high for admission. 

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a bar-preparation program that has a strong track record of helping students with similar profiles. Raising your demonstrated ability in law-school-level work will be the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
